cup-and-ring-mark.name: Cup and ring marks
cup-and-ring-mark.summary: Prehistoric rock art consisting of concentric circles pecked into stone, found along the Atlantic coast from Ireland and Britain to Spain and Portugal, and in parts of the Mediterranean.

galicia-spain.name: Galicia
galicia-spain.summary: An autonomous community in northwest Spain named after the Celtic Gallaeci people, incorporated into the Roman Empire in 19 BC and later ruled by Suebi and Visigoth kingdoms.

atlantic-bronze-age.name: Atlantic Bronze Age
atlantic-bronze-age.summary: Term for a Bronze Age period or cultural complex, roughly 1300 to 700 BC, along the Atlantic coasts of Britain, France, Ireland, Portugal and Spain.

boscawen-un.name: Boscawen-Un
boscawen-un.summary: A Bronze Age stone circle near St Buryan in Cornwall, made up of nineteen upright stones arranged in an ellipse.

bell-beaker-culture.name: Bell Beaker culture
bell-beaker-culture.summary: A Bronze Age archaeological culture named for its inverted-bell drinking vessel, spreading across Western Europe from around 2800 BCE.

early-european-farmers.name: Early European Farmers
early-european-farmers.summary: A population that carried farming from Anatolia into Europe and Northwest Africa from around 7,000 BC, gradually mixing with local hunter-gatherer groups.

western-steppe-herders.name: Western Steppe Herders
western-steppe-herders.summary: A genetic ancestry group first identified in Chalcolithic steppe populations around 5000 BC, descended from a merger of Eastern and Caucasus hunter-gatherers, later spreading widely across Eurasia.

chalcolithic.name: Chalcolithic (Copper Age)
chalcolithic.summary: An archaeological period between the Neolithic and Bronze Age marked by growing use of smelted copper, with evidence of copper smelting from as early as about 5000 BCE in parts of Europe.

amesbury-archer.name: Amesbury Archer
amesbury-archer.summary: A Bronze Age man buried near Stonehenge around 2300 BC with an unusually rich array of grave goods, including the earliest gold objects found in England, showing surprising social hierarchy for the period.

boscombe-bowmen.name: Boscombe Bowmen
boscombe-bowmen.summary: The name archaeologists gave to a group of early Bronze Age Bell Beaker people found in a shared burial at Boscombe Down near Stonehenge, Wiltshire.

p-mmelte.name: Pömmelte
p-mmelte.summary: A village in Germany, now part of the town Barby, where prehistoric dwelling structures dating from 2800 to 2200 BC, linked to the Bell Beaker and Unetice cultures, have been identified.

woodhenge.name: Woodhenge
woodhenge.summary: A Neolithic timber circle monument within the Stonehenge World Heritage Site in Wiltshire, England, about 2 miles northeast of Stonehenge.

stuart-piggott.name: Stuart Piggott
stuart-piggott.summary: A British archaeologist (1910 to 1996) best known for his work on prehistoric Wessex.

wessex-culture.name: Wessex culture
wessex-culture.summary: The leading prehistoric culture of early Bronze Age central and southern Britain, linked to trade networks across Europe and to the later phases of Stonehenge's construction.

armorican-tumulus-culture.name: Armorican Tumulus culture
armorican-tumulus-culture.summary: Bronze Age culture of western Brittany known for over a thousand burial mounds, including richly furnished chieftains' graves contemporary with England's Wessex culture.

n-tice-culture.name: Únětice culture
n-tice-culture.summary: An archaeological culture at the start of the Central European Bronze Age, dated to about 2300 to 1600 BC, known from sites across the Czech Republic, Slovakia, Poland and Germany.

hilversum-culture.name: Hilversum culture
hilversum-culture.summary: A prehistoric Bronze Age material culture of the southern Netherlands and northern Belgium, linked to the Wessex culture of southern England from the same period.

avanton.name: Avanton
avanton.summary: A commune in western France, near where a Bronze Age golden hat known as the Avanton Gold Cone was found in 1844.

gold-hat.name: Gold hats
gold-hat.summary: Four known cone-shaped Bronze Age European artifacts, made of thin sheet gold worn over tall conical headdresses, dated to roughly 1400–800 BC.

seahenge.name: Seahenge
seahenge.summary: A prehistoric timber circle in Norfolk, England, built in 2049 BC alongside the nearby Holme II circle, likely for ritual purposes; excavated in 1999 due to coastal erosion.

callanish-stones.name: Calanais Stones
callanish-stones.summary: A Neolithic stone circle and alignment on Scotland's Isle of Lewis, built around 2750 BC and used for ceremonial activity for centuries into the Bronze Age.

newgrange.name: Newgrange
newgrange.summary: A Neolithic passage tomb in County Meath, Ireland, built around 3100 BC, older than Stonehenge and the Egyptian pyramids, aligned so sunlight floods its chamber at the winter solstice.

county-meath.name: County Meath
county-meath.summary: A county in eastern Ireland known as 'The Royal County,' once the seat of Ireland's High Kings before being formally shired in 1297.

timothy-darvill.name: Timothy Darvill
timothy-darvill.summary: English archaeologist (1957–2024) known for work on prehistoric Britain, including a 2008 Stonehenge excavation featured in a BBC programme that explored the theory that the site was used for healing.

geoffrey-wainwright-archaeologist.name: Geoffrey Wainwright
geoffrey-wainwright-archaeologist.summary: British archaeologist specialising in prehistory (1937–2017), who served as Chief Archaeologist of English Heritage from 1989 to 1999 and led leading prehistoric and antiquarian societies.

excarnation.name: Excarnation
excarnation.summary: The archaeological term for removing flesh and organs from the dead before burial, practiced worldwide for spiritual or practical reasons, such as sky burials.

michael-j-o-kelly.name: Michael J. O'Kelly
michael-j-o-kelly.summary: An Irish archaeologist (1915–1982) who led the excavation and restoration of Newgrange, the Neolithic passage tomb now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

knowth.name: Knowth
knowth.summary: A prehistoric passage tomb near the River Boyne in Ireland, built around 3200 BC and holding Europe's largest collection of megalithic art, part of the Brú na Bóinne World Heritage Site.

dowth.name: Dowth
dowth.summary: A Neolithic passage tomb near the River Boyne in Ireland, one of three main tombs of the Brú na Bóinne site along with Newgrange and Knowth, dating to about 3200 BC.

grooved-ware.name: Grooved ware
grooved-ware.summary: A style of flat-bottomed, grooved pottery from Neolithic Britain, first developed in Orkney in the early 3rd millennium BC and often linked to ritual sites.

loughcrew.name: Loughcrew
loughcrew.summary: A hilltop group of passage tombs from the 4th millennium BCE near Oldcastle, Ireland, with rare megalithic art; one of Ireland's four main passage tomb cemeteries.

avebury.name: Avebury
avebury.summary: A Neolithic henge monument in Wiltshire, England, containing the largest megalithic stone circle in the world, built during the third millennium BC.

silbury-hill.name: Silbury Hill
silbury-hill.summary: A prehistoric artificial chalk mound near Avebury, England, standing 39.3 metres tall, the largest man-made mound of its kind in Europe.

promontory-fort.name: Cliff castles
promontory-fort.summary: A defensive structure built above a steep cliff, using the terrain to reduce the ramparts needed; mainly found in Ireland, Brittany, and other Atlantic coastal areas.

schifferstadt.name: Schifferstadt
schifferstadt.summary: Town in Rhineland-Palatinate, Germany, near Ludwigshafen and Speyer; the only urban municipality in its district besides Ludwigshafen itself.

ian-barnes-biologist.name: Ian Barnes
ian-barnes-biologist.summary: An evolutionary geneticist, born 1972, at London's Natural History Museum, known for pioneering the use of ancient DNA to study prehistoric human and animal populations.

berlin-gold-hat.name: Berlin Gold Hat
berlin-gold-hat.summary: A Late Bronze Age gold-leaf artefact covering a conical headdress, likely insignia in a sun cult and possibly used for calendar purposes, dated to about 1000–800 BC.

metonic-cycle.name: Metonic cycle
metonic-cycle.summary: A roughly 19-year cycle after which lunar phases recur on the same calendar dates, identified by the Greek astronomer Meton of Athens in the 5th century BCE and used in lunisolar calendars.
